objectives.summary: Storage account hardening comes down to a handful of account-level settings: secure transfer (HTTPS), minimum TLS version, blob anonymous access, Shared Key authorization, and the encryption options. The exam often tests the defaults, especially those that differ between the portal and CLI/ARM. It also tests what each setting overrides and which roles can change it, so it's worth knowing that Storage Account Contributor can list the account keys.

keyFacts.fact: If AllowSharedKeyAccess isn't set (null) or is true, the account accepts Shared Key requests. Setting it to false rejects requests signed with the account key with 403. Only Microsoft Entra ID requests, plus user delegation SAS where applicable, are accepted.

The portal sets MinimumTlsVersion to TLS 1.2 by default. PowerShell, Azure CLI and ARM templates leave the property unset, so it returns no value until you configure it explicitly. TLS 1.3 can be negotiated but can't be set as the minimum.

Setting AllowBlobPublicAccess to false overrides the anonymous access setting of every container in the account. The $web static website container is unaffected and always public. Containers default to no public read access (Private).
Owner, Contributor and Storage Account Contributor can change these account settings, and all three include listkeys/action, which gives full data access through the account keys.
Infrastructure encryption (double encryption) has to be enabled when the account is created. Customer-managed keys can be stored in Azure Key Vault or Managed HSM.
To protect a storage account with Microsoft Entra Conditional Access policies, you must disallow Shared Key authorization on the account.

Azure Storage stopped supporting TLS 1.0 and 1.1 on February 3, 2026, for new and existing accounts; TLS 1.2 is now the effective minimum. Older guidance saying an unset account accepts TLS 1.0 predates this retirement.

objectives.portalPath: Storage account > Settings > Configuration (Secure transfer required, Allow Blob anonymous access, Allow storage account key access, Minimum TLS version); Security + networking > Encryption

lab.title: Harden a storage account with Azure CLI
steps: In Cloud Shell, create a storage account: az storage account create --name <unique> --resource-group <rg> --kind StorageV2 --location eastus --allow-blob-public-access false
Check the TLS setting: az storage account show --name <unique> --resource-group <rg> --query minimumTlsVersion (with CLI it may come back empty).
Set TLS 1.2: az storage account update --name <unique> --resource-group <rg> --min-tls-version TLS1_2
Disable Shared Key: az storage account update --name <unique> --resource-group <rg> --allow-shared-key-access false
Verify: az storage account show --name <unique> --resource-group <rg> --query "{tls:minimumTlsVersion, sharedKey:allowSharedKeyAccess, anon:allowBlobPublicAccess}"
Try listing containers with key auth: az storage container list --account-name <unique> --auth-mode key
lab.verify: The query returns TLS1_2, false and false. The key-based container list fails with an error saying key-based authorization isn't permitted. The same command with --auth-mode login works if you hold a blob data role.

objectives.summary: The storage firewall restricts the public endpoint with four kinds of rules: virtual network rules (which rely on service endpoints), public IP rules, resource instance rules, and the trusted Azure services exception. Exam questions focus on rule limits, the restrictions on IP rules, what each rule type actually grants, and how much precedence trusted services get.

keyFacts.fact: The four network rule types are virtual network rules, IP network rules, resource instance rules and trusted service exceptions. Each storage account supports up to 400 IP network rules and up to 400 virtual network rules.

IP rules accept public IPv4 addresses only. RFC 1918 private ranges aren't allowed, /31 and /32 prefixes have to be entered as single addresses, and IP rules have no effect on requests from the same Azure region as the account.

A resource instance rule opens the public endpoint to a specific Azure resource, which must be in the same tenant but can be in any subscription. It doesn't grant data access, so the resource's managed identity still needs an Azure role.

Microsoft recommends resource instance rules over the broad 'Allow Azure services on the trusted services list' exception because they create a smaller trust surface. The exception covers only documented service scenarios and doesn't open the account to all of Azure.

Trusted service access has the highest precedence. If you switch Public network access from 'selected networks' to Disabled, existing resource instance rules and exceptions, trusted services included, stay in effect.

Firewall rules apply only to data-plane operations, not control-plane operations. Enabling a service endpoint on a subnet switches its traffic to a private source IP, so IP rules for that subnet's old public IP stop working.

objectives.portalPath: Storage account > Security + networking > Networking > Public network access (Manage) and Resource settings: Virtual networks, IP addresses, and exceptions > View

lab.title: Restrict a storage account to your IP and one resource instance
steps: Open the storage account > Security + networking > Networking. Under Public network access select Manage > Enable > Enabled from selected networks, and save.
Under Resource settings: Virtual networks, IP addresses, and exceptions, select View. In the IP box, add your client's public IPv4 address, not a 10.x/192.168.x private address.
In the Resource instances section, choose a Resource type (for example Microsoft.DataFactory/factories) and an instance, and save.
From Cloud Shell, list a resource instance rule: az storage account network-rule list -g <rg> --account-name <account>
From a machine whose IP isn't allowed, try to list blobs in a container.
lab.verify: The network-rule list output shows the IP rule and the resourceAccessRules entry. Data access from your allowed IP works, while access from other networks returns 403 (AuthorizationFailure).

flashcards.back: No. IP rules accept public IPv4 only, and RFC 1918 ranges aren't allowed. Use a virtual network rule or a private endpoint instead.

flashcards.back: No. It opens network access only. Its managed identity still needs an Azure role, such as Storage Blob Data Reader.

questions.scenario: Contoso's storage account stdata01 allows only selected networks. A single Azure Synapse workspace, Synapse1, in another subscription of the same tenant must read blobs through its system-assigned managed identity. Security wants the smallest possible trust surface.
questions.question: Which network configuration should you add?
options: Enable 'Allow Azure services on the trusted services list to access this storage account'.
Add a resource instance rule for Synapse1.
Add an IP network rule for Synapse1's outbound public IP address.
Set Public network access to Enabled from all networks.
questions.explanation: A resource instance rule authorizes one named resource, and Microsoft recommends it over the trusted services exception because the trust surface is smaller. Resource instances can come from any subscription in the same tenant. The trusted services exception would admit qualifying instances broadly rather than just Synapse1. IP rules don't apply to Azure services in the same region and aren't reliable for Azure-hosted services. Opening the account to all networks removes the restriction entirely.

Storage account stlogs01 is in East US and allows only selected networks. stlogs01 has an IP network rule for VM1's public IP address, and VM1 can read blobs. An engineer then enables the Microsoft.Storage.Global service endpoint on Subnet1, and VM1 starts getting 403 errors.
questions.question: What should you do to restore access?
options: Add a virtual network rule for Subnet1 on stlogs01.
Add VM1's private IP address as an IP network rule.
Enable the trusted services exception on stlogs01.
Delete and re-create the IP network rule for VM1's public IP address.
questions.explanation: Once a subnet has a storage service endpoint (Microsoft.Storage.Global covers accounts in any region), its storage traffic uses a private source IP, so the IP rule for VM1's public address no longer matches. A virtual network rule for Subnet1 fixes it, and VNet rules can reference subnets in any region. Private (RFC 1918) addresses can't be used in IP rules. The trusted services exception covers specific Azure services, not your VMs. Re-creating the same public IP rule changes nothing, because the traffic no longer comes from that address.

objectives.summary: Defender for Storage (the current plan, priced per storage account) has three parts. Activity monitoring is always on. Malware scanning is billed per GB, runs on upload or on demand, and is powered by Microsoft Defender Antivirus. Sensitive data threat detection is free with the plan. You need to know the defaults, the monthly scan cap, the ways scan results are delivered and their prerequisites, and how to override subscription-level settings for one account.

keyFacts.fact: Enabling the plan at subscription level in the portal turns on on-upload malware scanning and sensitive data threat detection by default. Sensitive data threat detection adds no cost, while malware scanning is billed per GB scanned.

On-upload scanning has a default cap of 10,000 GB (10 TB) per storage account per month. Scanning stops once the cap is reached, give or take about 20 GB, and the cap resets at midnight UTC at the end of each month.

Scan results go to blob index tags (on by default, but not tamper-resistant) and to Defender for Cloud alerts. You can also send them to an Event Grid custom topic for near-real-time automation, which must be in the same region as the storage account, allow public network access and use the Event Grid schema. A Log Analytics workspace stores them in the StorageMalwareScanningResults table.
The built-in 'soft delete malicious blobs' remediation is off by default. If blob soft delete isn't already on, turning the feature on enables it, with a default retention of 7 days (range 1–365).

To give one storage account settings that differ from the subscription, such as its own Event Grid topic or a different cap, set 'Override Defender for Storage subscription-level settings' to On for that account.

Sensitive data threat detection runs an agentless sampling engine that uses Microsoft Purview sensitive information types. Results usually arrive within 24 hours, new accounts are scanned within 6 hours, and rescans happen weekly.
Defender for Cloud raises an alert when an account reaches 75% of its monthly scan cap and another when the cap is reached and scanning stops for the rest of the month.
On-upload malware scanning requires the Microsoft.EventGrid resource provider to be registered, and enabling it creates an Event Grid system topic in the storage account's resource group.

objectives.portalPath: Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > subscription > Defender plans > Storage > Settings / Edit configuration; Storage account > Security + networking > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Settings

lab.title: Send malware scan results to Log Analytics and test with EICAR
steps: Register the Microsoft.EventGrid resource provider in your trial subscription, then enable Defender for Storage on a test storage account: storage account > Security + networking > Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Enable on storage account.
Create a Log Analytics workspace in the same subscription.

In the storage account's Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Settings, set 'Override Defender for Storage subscription-level settings' to On, set the GB-per-month limit to 50, choose the workspace as the scan results destination, and save.
Upload the EICAR antimalware test file (a harmless standard test string) to a container.
Open the blob's Index tags and look at the scan result tag.
In the workspace, run: StorageMalwareScanningResults | take 10
lab.verify: The blob's index tags show the result as Malicious, a Defender for Cloud security alert appears, and the StorageMalwareScanningResults table contains the scan record. The table is created when the first result is recorded.

objectives.summary: Delegated access to Azure Storage relies on shared access signatures. A user delegation SAS is signed with Entra credentials, and a service SAS or account SAS is signed with the account key. A stored access policy gives you server-side control and a way to revoke service SAS tokens. The exam tests which SAS types can use stored access policies, how to revoke each type, the limits (five policies and seven days), and the least-privileged role needed to create a user delegation SAS.

keyFacts.fact: There are three SAS types. A user delegation SAS is signed with a user delegation key from Microsoft Entra ID and is the type Microsoft recommends. A service SAS covers one storage service and is signed with the account key. An account SAS covers one or more services, including service-level operations, and is also signed with the account key.

Stored access policies work only with a service SAS. A user delegation SAS or account SAS must be an ad hoc SAS. Blob containers, file shares, queues and tables each support up to five stored access policies, and a sixth returns 400 (Bad Request).

A start time, expiry time or permission can be set on the SAS token or on the stored access policy, not on both. A new or changed policy can take up to 30 seconds to take effect, and requests may get 403 in the meantime.

To revoke a service SAS tied to a stored access policy, delete the policy, change its expiry to the past, or rename its identifier. Recreating a policy under the same name revives old tokens. An ad hoc service or account SAS can be revoked only by regenerating the account key that signed it.

A user delegation key, and so any SAS it signs, is valid for at most 7 days. Revoking the user delegation keys (az storage account revoke-delegation-keys) invalidates every SAS they signed, though caching can delay the effect.

Requesting a user delegation key needs generateUserDelegationKey at storage account, resource group or subscription scope. The least-privileged built-in role is Storage Blob Delegator, which you can add for a principal whose data role is scoped only to a container.

objectives.portalPath: Storage account > Data storage > Containers > select container > ... > Access policy > Stored access policies > + Add policy; Container or blob > Generate SAS

lab.title: Create, use and revoke a stored-access-policy SAS
steps: In the portal, open a storage account > Containers. Select a container, then ... > Access policy.
Under Stored access policies, select + Add policy. Set Identifier to policy-read, permission to Read, and an expiry one day out, then OK and Save.
Upload a test file to the container. On the blob, select Generate SAS, choose Signing method: Account key and Stored access policy: policy-read, then generate the SAS URL.
Open the SAS URL in a browser to confirm the download works.
Return to Access policy and delete policy-read (or rename its identifier), then save. Wait about 30 seconds.
Open the same SAS URL again.
lab.verify: Before you remove the policy the blob downloads. Afterwards the same URL fails with an authentication error, which shows the SAS was revoked without regenerating the account keys.

flashcards.front: Which SAS type can be associated with a stored access policy?
flashcards.back: Only a service SAS. User delegation and account SAS must be ad hoc.

flashcards.front: What is the maximum lifetime of a user delegation SAS?
flashcards.back: 7 days, the maximum lifetime of the user delegation key that signs it.

flashcards.front: How many stored access policies can a container have?
flashcards.back: Five. A sixth fails with 400 (Bad Request).

questions.scenario: Contoso gives a partner a SAS for container invoices. If the token leaks, it must be possible to revoke it quickly without breaking other applications that use the storage account keys, and without changing the partner's Entra permissions. Shared Key access is allowed on the account.
questions.question: Which type of SAS should you issue?
options: An ad hoc account SAS
A service SAS associated with a stored access policy on the invoices container
An ad hoc service SAS with a one-year expiry
An account SAS associated with a stored access policy
questions.explanation: A service SAS bound to a stored access policy can be revoked by deleting or changing the policy, so the account keys don't need regenerating. An ad hoc account or service SAS can be revoked only by regenerating the key that signed it, which would break the other applications, and a one-year expiry makes the exposure worse. Account SAS can't use stored access policies at all.

questions.scenario: App1 runs with a managed identity that has Storage Blob Data Reader scoped to container reports in stcorp01. App1 must issue read-only user delegation SAS tokens for blobs in reports. Calls to Get User Delegation Key currently fail. Your solution must follow the principle of least privilege.
questions.question: Which additional role assignment should you make for App1's managed identity?
options: Storage Blob Delegator at the stcorp01 storage account scope
Storage Blob Delegator at the reports container scope
Storage Account Contributor at the stcorp01 scope
Storage Blob Data Owner at the reports container scope
questions.explanation: Get User Delegation Key works at storage account level, so generateUserDelegationKey has to be granted at account, resource group or subscription scope. Storage Blob Delegator is the least-privileged built-in role with that action, and Learn suggests adding it when the data role is scoped to a container. A container-scoped assignment doesn't cover the account-level operation. Storage Account Contributor would also grant listkeys and management rights. A container-scoped Data Owner still lacks the action at account scope and adds write permissions.

statements.text: A user delegation SAS created with an expiry 30 days in the future stays valid for 30 days.
If you delete a stored access policy and then recreate it with the same name, SAS tokens issued under the old policy become valid again (if they haven't expired).
You can specify the expiry time both in the SAS token and in its stored access policy.

Old tokens are valid again under a policy with the same name, so use a new name when you recreate a policy to revoke access.
